entry:
Physiological damage to an organism caused by mechanical trauma, toxins, interactions with other organisms, or abiotic environmental factors.

In animals, injury is sometimes defined as mechanical damage to an anatomical structure, but the wider sense covers physical damage from any cause, including drowning, [[Burn|burns]], and poisoning. Such damage may result from attempted predation, territorial fights, falls, and abiotic factors. In animals of many phyla, injury triggers an inflammatory response that prompts coagulation of blood or body fluid, followed by [[Wound|wound]] healing, which may be rapid, as in [[Cnidaria|cnidarians]]. Annelids, arthropods, cnidarians, molluscs, nematodes, and vertebrates produce antimicrobial peptides to fight infection afterward.

Much of medical practice, including emergency medicine and pain management, is devoted to treating human injuries. The [[World Health Organization]] classifies them by mechanism, objects or substances producing injury, place of occurrence, activity when injured, and the role of human intent. Injuries can also cause psychological harm, including [[Post-traumatic stress disorder|post-traumatic stress disorder]].

In plants, injuries result from consumption by [[Herbivore|herbivores]], damage by pathogens such as bacteria and fungi, and abiotic factors such as heat, freezing, flooding, lightning, and pollutants such as ozone. Plants signal damage, secrete materials that seal the area, produce antimicrobial chemicals, and, in woody species, regrow over wounds. In fungi with septate hyphae, an injured hypha can block its septal pores; in the Mucoromycota, which mostly lack septa, the protoplasm forms a gel. Some fungi regenerate damaged hyphae, and others produce reproductive conidia in response to damage.

Plants, animals, fungi, and single-celled eukaryotes such as choanoflagellates share many response mechanisms, including calcium-ion signalling, reactive oxygen species, and extracellular [[Adenosine triphosphate|adenosine triphosphate]] detected by P2X receptors. This sharing implies that the mechanisms are ancient. Thibaut Brunet and Detlev Arendt propose that the last eukaryotic common ancestor had a calcium-based healing response that detected an inflow of calcium ions and sealed openings in the [[Cell membrane|cell membrane]] by exocytosis.

Branch of chemistry that studies the preparation, properties, and behavior of inorganic and organometallic compounds, mainly those not based on carbon.

Unlike [[Organic chemistry]], it deals chiefly with non-carbon compounds, though the fields overlap, especially in [[Organometallic chemistry|organometallic chemistry]]. Its products are used in catalysts, materials, paints and pigments, coatings, medicines, fuels, and agriculture. Many inorganic compounds occur naturally as minerals, such as iron sulfide as [[Pyrite|pyrite]]. Others serve as biomolecules: electrolytes such as [[Sodium chloride|sodium chloride]], ATP for energy storage, and the polyphosphate backbone of DNA.

Inorganic compounds may be ionic, as in magnesium chloride (MgCl₂), which contains Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions; covalent, with shared electrons; or polar covalent, common in oxides, carbonates, and halides. Many have high melting points, and some ionic compounds, such as NaCl, dissolve easily in water. Acid-base behavior is described by Lewis theory and refined by HSAB theory. Subdivisions include organometallic, cluster, bioinorganic, materials, and solid-state chemistry.

Classical coordination compounds feature metals bound to lone pairs on ligands such as H₂O, NH₃, Cl⁻, and CN⁻. Structures range from tetrahedral for titanium to square planar for some nickel complexes and octahedral for cobalt complexes. Transition metals occur in biologically important compounds, such as iron in [[Hemoglobin|hemoglobin]]. Alfred Werner's work on coordination theory earned him the 1913 Nobel Prize in Chemistry; his separation of enantiomers of a cobalt complex showed that chirality is not inherent to organic compounds.

The field is highly practical. Traditionally, the scale of a nation's economy could be gauged by its output of [[Sulfuric acid|sulfuric acid]]. Ammonium nitrate, used as fertilizer, depends on ammonia made by the [[Haber process]], whose practical synthesis with iron catalysts was achieved by Carl Bosch and [[Fritz Haber]] in the early 1900s. Portland cement is another large-scale inorganic material, and vanadium(V) oxide and titanium(III) chloride serve as industrial catalysts.

Invertebrate class (Insecta) of the phylum Arthropoda, the most diverse group of animals.

Insects have an exoskeleton, a body of head, thorax, and abdomen, three pairs of jointed legs, compound eyes, and a pair of antennae. More than a million species have been described, more than half of all animal species; estimates suggest about 5.5 million exist. The orders Hemiptera, Lepidoptera, Diptera, Hymenoptera, and Coleoptera each have more than 100,000 described species. Insects occur on every continent and in almost every terrestrial habitat, with many more species in the tropics than in temperate zones. The name comes from Latin *insectum*, "cut up", introduced by [[Pliny the Elder]] as a translation of Aristotle's Greek term.

The nervous system consists of a brain and a ventral nerve cord. Insects breathe through paired openings along their sides connected to small tubes, so the blood does not carry oxygen. Most reproduce by laying eggs, and growth involves a series of molts. Four-stage [[Metamorphosis|metamorphosis]] includes a nearly immobile pupa; three-stage metamorphosis lacks one, and the young develop through nymphal stages. Insects are the only invertebrates capable of sustained powered flight, which evolved just once. Bees, ants, and [[Termite|termites]] live in large colonies. Male moths sense the [[Pheromone|pheromones]] of females over great distances, crickets stridulate, and lampyrid beetles communicate with light.

Fossil insects from the [[Paleozoic]] include dragonfly-like forms with wingspans of 55 to 70 cm. The most diverse groups appear to have coevolved with [[Flowering plant|flowering plants]]. Humans regard many insects as pests, especially those damaging crops, and some are parasites or disease vectors. Pollinators are essential to the reproduction of many flowering plants, and many insects prey on pests. Silkworms and the [[Honey bee|honey bee]] were domesticated for silk and honey, and insects are eaten in 80% of the world's nations by roughly 3,000 ethnic groups. Human activities are seriously affecting insect biodiversity.

Means of protection from financial loss in which, for a fee, one party agrees to compensate another for a certain loss, damage, or injury.

A form of risk management, it protects against contingent or uncertain loss. The insurer, also called an insurance company, carrier, or underwriter, issues a policy detailing when it will compensate the insured or a designated beneficiary. The policyholder pays a premium, accepting a small known loss in exchange for the promise of compensation, usually for something in which the insured has an insurable interest. After a loss, the insured submits a claim, processed by a claims adjuster; a deductible is the out-of-pocket expense required before the insurer pays. Insurers may take out reinsurance to share large risks, and rely on the [[Law of large numbers|law of large numbers]] to forecast aggregate losses.

Methods of distributing risk were practiced by Chinese and Indian traders in the 3rd and 2nd millennia BC. Codex Hammurabi Law 238 (c. 1755–1750 BC) set rules for sharing the loss of ships. The Lex Rhodia, the general average principle of marine insurance, was established on [[Rhodes]] in approximately 1000 to 800 BC and was preserved in the *Digesta* ordered by [[Justinian I]] in 533. Ancient Greeks made marine loans repayable only if the voyage prospered. Direct insurance of sea risks for a premium began in [[Belgium]] about 1300 AD, and separate insurance contracts were invented in [[Genoa]] in the 14th century; the first known dates from 1347. The earliest known life insurance policy was made at the Royal Exchange, [[London]], on June 18, 1583, for £383, 6s. 8d. on the life of William Gibbons.

Property insurance can be traced to the [[Great Fire of London]] in 1666, which destroyed more than 13,000 houses. In 1681 Nicholas Barbon and eleven associates established the first fire insurance company, the "Insurance Office for Houses". Insurance faces problems such as moral hazard, in which insured parties may take more risks, and insurer insolvency during correlated losses. Regulation developed to enforce solvency, transparency, and fair practices.

Number that is zero, a positive natural number, or the negation of a positive natural number.

The negations of the positive natural numbers (−1, −2, −3, ...) are the negative integers. The set of all integers is denoted by Z or ℤ, from the German *Zahlen*, "numbers", a usage attributed to [[David Hilbert]]. It contains the [[Natural number|natural numbers]] and is contained in the [[Rational number|rational numbers]] and the real numbers. Like the natural numbers, it is countably infinite. The numbers 21, 4, 0, and −2048 are integers; 9.75, 5/4, and the square root of 2 are not. In algebraic number theory, integers are sometimes called rational integers to distinguish them from algebraic integers.

The word is Latin for "whole" or "untouched". Historically only positive integers were considered, and the definition widened as negative numbers proved useful. Negative numbers first appear in Chinese mathematics between 200 BC and 200 AD, and Indian texts of about the 7th century AD set rules for operating with them. [[Leonhard Euler]] defined integers to include negatives in his 1765 *Elements of Algebra*. The phrase "the set of the integers" was not used before the end of the 19th century, when [[Georg Cantor]] introduced set theory. The letter Z appeared in a textbook in Nicolas Bourbaki's *Algèbre* in 1947, and was generally used by modern algebra texts by 1961. Whether "whole numbers" includes negatives remains ambiguous.

The integers are closed under addition, multiplication, and subtraction, but not under division or exponentiation. Under addition they form an [[Abelian group]], the only infinite cyclic group up to isomorphism. Under multiplication they form a commutative monoid, since not every integer has a multiplicative inverse. With both operations they form a commutative [[Ring (mathematics)|ring]] with unity, the smallest ring containing the natural numbers, and an integral domain because they lack zero divisors. They do not form a [[Field (mathematics)|field]]; the smallest field containing them is the rational numbers.

Neurodevelopmental disorder marked by significant impairment in intellectual and adaptive functioning.

Also called disorder of intellectual development, and known as learning difficulty in the United Kingdom, it usually becomes apparent in infancy, early childhood, or school age. Affected children typically have an [[Intelligence quotient|intelligence quotient]] (IQ) below 70 and deficits in at least two adaptive behaviors affecting everyday living. According to the DSM-5, intellectual functions include reasoning, problem solving, planning, abstract thinking, judgment, academic learning, and learning from experience; deficits must be confirmed by clinical evaluation and standardized IQ testing. Adaptive behaviors are the social, developmental, and practical skills used in daily life. Age-related decline in memory and cognition, as in [[Alzheimer's disease]], can also cause it.

The disorder is subdivided into syndromic forms, accompanied by other medical and behavioral signs, as in [[Down syndrome]] and fragile X syndrome, and non-syndromic forms without other abnormalities. Estimates of prevalence range from about 1% of the global population to 2–3%, reflecting differences in diagnostic criteria and ascertainment. Causes include genetic disorders, which account for about a quarter of cases, with about 5% inherited; prenatal exposure such as fetal alcohol exposure; perinatal complications; and postnatal infections or trauma. The cause is unidentified in up to half of cases.

Severity ranges from mild to profound. About 85% of people with the disorder have mild forms, and about 10% moderate; severe accounts for 3.5% and profound for 1.5%. People with mild disability can learn reading and mathematics to about the level of a typical child aged nine to twelve, and many live independently and hold jobs as adults. Those with moderate disability need considerable support at school, at home, and in the community. Those with severe or profound disability need intensive support and supervision throughout life.

The condition often co-occurs with [[Autism|autism]]: roughly 30% of those with autism spectrum disorder also have intellectual disability, which can complicate diagnosis.

Capacity to perceive or infer information and retain it as knowledge to be applied to adaptive behavior within an environment or context.

It has been defined in many ways: as the capacity for abstraction, logic, understanding, self-awareness, learning, emotional knowledge, reasoning, planning, creativity, critical thinking, and problem-solving. A 1995 report of the American Psychological Association, *Intelligence: Knowns and Unknowns*, noted that when two dozen prominent theorists were asked to define it, they gave two dozen somewhat different definitions. The term rose to prominence in the early 1900s, and most psychologists believe intelligence divides into various domains or competencies. It has also been observed in the cognition of non-human animals; some researchers suggest that plants show forms of intelligence, though this remains controversial.

The word derives from the Latin *intelligentia* or *intellectus*, from *intelligere*, "to comprehend or perceive". In the [[Middle Ages]], *intellectus* became the scholarly term for understanding and a translation of the Greek *nous*. Early modern philosophers including [[Francis Bacon]], [[Thomas Hobbes]], [[John Locke]], and [[David Hume]] rejected the scholastic theories attached to it and preferred "understanding".

Human intelligence includes the abilities to learn, form concepts, reason, recognize patterns, innovate, plan, solve problems, and use language. These abilities are organized in frameworks such as fluid versus crystallized intelligence and the Cattell-Horn-Carroll model. Intelligence is distinct from learning, the retention of facts and abilities.

Psychometric attempts to quantify intelligence include [[Intelligence quotient|IQ]] tests, first developed in the early 20th century to screen children for [[Intellectual disability|intellectual disability]] and later used to screen immigrants, military recruits, and job applicants. The *g* factor summarizes correlations among scores on cognitive tests; Grokipedia-style claims aside, the source attributes it to Charles Spearman in 1904. Most psychologists agree IQ measures some aspects of intelligence, particularly performance in academic contexts, while many question its validity as a measure of intelligence as a whole. Twin and adoption studies estimate heritability of individual differences at about 20–40% in childhood and 50–80% in adulthood, and the balance of genetic and environmental influences is debated. Researchers also disagree about average group differences in scores; one widely cited view holds that genetics does not explain average differences between racial groups, while others argue such differences are partly heritable.

Heat engine in which fuel burns with an oxidizer, usually air, in a combustion chamber that is an integral part of the working fluid flow circuit.

The expansion of high-temperature, high-pressure gases from [[Combustion|combustion]] applies direct force to pistons, turbine blades, a rotor, or a nozzle, converting chemical energy into kinetic energy. The term usually means engines with intermittent combustion, such as two-stroke and four-stroke piston engines and the [[Wankel engine]]. A second class uses continuous combustion: gas turbines, jet engines, and most rocket engines. In external combustion engines, such as the [[Steam engine|steam]] and [[Stirling engine|Stirling]] engines, energy is delivered to a working fluid not mixed with combustion products.

Most such engines are used in mobile applications, as the primary power for cars, aircraft, and boats. They run on hydrocarbon fuels such as natural gas, gasoline, diesel fuel, or ethanol; biodiesel and bioethanol are renewable alternatives, and hydrogen is rarely used. By 1900 Rudolf Diesel was running engines on peanut oil. Thermal efficiencies range from 20% to 40% depending on design and load.

Many inventors contributed. In 1807 French engineers Nicéphore Niépce and Claude Niépce ran the Pyréolophore, patented by [[Napoleon]], on a boat on the Saône, and François Isaac de Rivaz built a hydrogen-fueled engine, fitted to a primitive vehicle in 1808. Jean Joseph Etienne Lenoir produced a gas-fired engine in 1860. In 1864 [[Nicolaus Otto]] patented the first atmospheric gas engine, and in 1876 the compressed-charge, four-cycle Otto engine, the first modern internal combustion engine. Karl Benz patented a two-stroke gasoline engine in 1879 and began commercial production of motor vehicles in 1886. In 1892 [[Rudolf Diesel]] developed the first compression-ignition engine. Robert Goddard launched the first liquid-fueled rocket in 1926, and the Heinkel He 178 became the first jet aircraft in 1939.

Exhaust includes carbon dioxide, nitrogen oxides, particulate matter, and unburnt hydrocarbons, contributing to air pollution. Catalytic converters, fuel standards, and engine controls have sharply reduced some pollutants, while carbon dioxide emissions have prompted a shift toward electrification and alternative fuels.

Layered variation of chemical and physical properties within the solid Earth.

Mechanically, it consists of a rigid lithosphere, a semi-fluid asthenosphere, a semi-fluid mesosphere, a liquid outer core, and a solid inner core. Chemically, it consists of a silicate crust, a ferromagnesian mantle, and an iron-nickel core whose flowing upper portion generates the [[Earth's magnetic field]]. The two schemes align only partially. Knowledge rests on topography and bathymetry, rock outcrops, samples brought up by volcanoes, seismic waves, gravitational and magnetic measurements, and experiments on crystalline solids at deep-interior pressures and temperatures. The layered model was deduced in the early 20th century chiefly from seismic waves. Earth's mass is about 6×10²⁴ kg and its average density 5.515 g/cm³.

The [[Crust (geology)|crust]] ranges from 5 to 70 km thick. Oceanic crust, 5–10 km thick, is dense and mafic, while continental crust is thicker, less dense, and felsic. The [[Lithosphere|lithosphere]] comprises the crust and uppermost mantle. At the Mohorovičić discontinuity, primary seismic waves speed up from 6.7–7.2 km/s, consistent with [[Basalt|basalt]], to 7.6–8.6 km/s. The oldest known mineral grains are about 4.4 billion years old, indicating a solid crust for at least that long.

The [[Earth's mantle|mantle]] extends to a depth of 2,890 km, making it the thickest layer, at 83.7% of Earth's volume; the crust is 0.6%. It is divided into upper and lower mantle by a transition zone, with the D″ layer at its base, where pressure is about 140 GPa. Though solid, its hot silicate rock flows over long timescales, and [[Convection|convection]] drives the motion of tectonic plates. The heat comes from radioactive decay and the planet's formation. Viscosity rises with depth from 10²¹ to 10²⁴ pascal-second.

The outer core, liquid iron and nickel alloy roughly 2,200–2,300 km thick, generates the magnetic field through convective motion. The solid inner core has a radius of about 1,220–1,250 km and temperatures up to 5,400°C.

headword: International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement
sort_key: international red cross and red crescent movement
entry:
Humanitarian movement with approximately 17 million volunteers, members, and staff worldwide.

It was founded to protect human life and health, ensure respect for all human beings, and prevent and alleviate suffering. It has seven fundamental principles: humanity, impartiality, neutrality, independence, voluntary service, unity, and universality. It comprises the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), and approximately 192 national societies. The ICRC supplies aid to war-affected areas, promotes humanitarian standards, and monitors compliance with the [[Geneva Conventions]]. The IFRC supports areas hit by famine, disease, and natural or man-made disasters, and coordinates aid among national societies. The emblems of the red cross, red crescent, and red crystal are protective symbols under international law.

In June 1859 the Swiss businessman Jean-Henri Dunant traveled to Italy to meet French emperor [[Napoleon III]]. He arrived at Solferino on the evening of June 24, after a battle in which about 40,000 soldiers on both sides died or were wounded in a single day, and devoted himself for several days to caring for the wounded. Back in [[Geneva]], he published *A Memory of Solferino* in 1862 at his own expense, advocating national voluntary relief societies and an international treaty protecting medics and field hospitals.

In 1863 Gustave Moynier introduced the book to the Geneva Society for Public Welfare, which formed a commission of five, including [[Henry Dunant|Dunant]], later named the International Committee for Relief to the Wounded. An international conference was held in Geneva on October 26–29, 1863, attended by 36 individuals. Its resolutions proposed national relief societies, neutrality for wounded soldiers, volunteer relief, and a common symbol, a white armlet bearing a red cross. On August 22, 1864, a diplomatic conference of sixteen countries adopted the First Geneva Convention.

The ICRC documented over 12 million prisoner-of-war cases in [[World War I]]. Critics have charged that its neutrality, and its cautious reports on atrocities to preserve access, limited its response during [[World War II]]; the Movement has described neutrality as essential to aid delivery.
